header.title: Census or Sample?
header.subtitle: Choosing how to collect data — and why a good sample doesn't have to be huge

meta.ac9-descriptor-text: distinguish between a population and a sample and investigate techniques for data collection including census, sampling, observation, experiment and using digital tools; make inferences about populations from samples
meta.lesson-focus: Choose between a census and a sample by weighing cost, accuracy and practicality — a well-chosen representative sample can be small.
meta.sa-conceptual-understanding: Valid inferences about populations can be made by drawing conclusions from representative samples

html.section0_intro: Three quick questions from earlier work — data types, a percentage, and the word for a whole group. They warm up the thinking you'll use today.
html.section_warmup:
A real decision that's secretly today's statistics.

Every five years the Australian Government runs the Census — by law, it tries to count every single person in the country on one night. It costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes years to process.

Yet a TV company can tell how many people watched the grand final by asking only a few thousand households — not the whole nation. And a company can guess how long its light globes last without burning out every globe it makes.

Statisticians make this choice constantly. A census collects data from every member of the population; a sample collects it from a representative subset. Today you'll learn to decide which one fits — by weighing cost, accuracy and practicality. The key idea: a well-chosen sample can be surprisingly small and still be trusted.
html.vocab_cards:
Population
Tap to flip
The whole group you want to learn about.
The population might be all Australian teenagers, or every biscuit made today.
Census
Tap to flip
Collecting data from every member of the population.
Counting every student in one class is a census.
Sample
Tap to flip
Collecting data from a subset of the population, then inferring about the whole.
Asking 2000 teenagers about screen-time to estimate all of them.
Representative
Tap to flip
A sample that reflects the population's mix, so conclusions carry across.
A representative sample of a school includes every year level, not just Year 12.
Bias
Tap to flip
When a sample over-represents one group, so it misleads about the population.
Surveying only the computer club about screen-time is biased.
html.sort_activity:
Where does each data-collection job belong?
Count every student in one Year 8 class Estimate average screen-time of all Australian teenagers Test whether each parachute opens reliably The national population count held every 5 years Check the ripeness of a 50-tonne truckload of mangoes Record the height of every player on one netball team

Census fits

Sample needed

💡 A census fits when the population is small and easy to reach, or when the law demands an exact count. A sample is needed when the population is too large, when a census is too costly, or when testing destroys the item (you can't open every parachute and still sell them).
html.worked_example:
Decide: a parachute factory must know whether its parachutes open reliably. Should it test every parachute (a census) or a representative sample?

1
Name the population and the variable
Say exactly what group we care about and what we're measuring.
Population = every parachute the factory makes.
Variable = does it open reliably when deployed?
2
Ask: is a census practical? (cost · accuracy · practicality)
Weigh what a census would actually cost here.
Testing a parachute means deploying it — the test uses it up.
A census would test (and destroy) 100% of the stock → none left to sell.
Cost of a census here = impossibly high. This is destructive testing.
3
Decide and justify
Because a census is impossible, take a representative sample and infer about the whole batch.
Test a representative sample (e.g. a fixed fraction from each production batch). If the sample opens reliably, we infer the whole population does — accepting a small, measured risk.
Decision Sample — destructive testing makes a census impossible

retrieval.q: A survey records each Year 8 student's favourite sport. Is "favourite sport" categorical or numerical data?
retrieval.hint: It sorts people into named groups (netball, soccer…), not numbers.

retrieval.q: In statistics, the whole group we want to learn about is called the ____.
retrieval.hint: It starts with 'p' and means everyone/everything in the group.

weDo.q: Step 1 — Name the population and the variable. Population = all Australian teenagers. What is the variable we want to measure? (answer in a few words)
weDo.hint: We want an average of something measured in hours each day.

weDo.q: Step 2 — Is a census practical? A census would survey every Australian teenager. Give the single biggest reason that is impractical: the population is too ____.
weDo.hint: There are millions of them — cost and time would be enormous.

weDo.q: Step 3 — Decide. Because a census is impractical, we take a representative ____ and infer the average for all teenagers.
weDo.hint: A subset chosen to reflect the whole population.

checkpoint.q:
Hinge question. A company makes 2 million light globes a year and wants the average lifetime (hours until each globe fails). Testing a globe means running it until it burns out. Which method should it use, and why?

A. Census — test every globe, because only measuring all of them can be accurate.
B. Sample — test a representative selection, because the test destroys each globe, so a census would leave none to sell.
C. Census — test every globe, because 2 million is so large that a sample would be too small to trust.
D. Sample — just test whichever globes are easiest to grab, because any small sample will do.

Type the letter of the best answer.
checkpoint.hint: Two things rule out a census here: the test is destructive AND the population is huge. Which option names the destructive problem without the 'samples must be huge' myth?

checkpoint.q: A teacher wants the eye colour of every student in her class of 28. It's quick and harmless. Best method — census or sample?
checkpoint.hint: The population is tiny and easy to reach, so you can include everyone.

practice1.q: The whole group you want to study is called the ____.
Collecting data from every member of the population is called a ____.
Collecting data from a representative subset is called a ____.
practice1.hint: Part of the population, not all of it.

practice1.q: Counting every student in your class of 25 — census or sample?
practice1.hint: Small, easy to reach — you can include everyone.

practice1.q: Estimating the average screen-time of all Australian teenagers — census or sample?
practice1.hint: Millions of people — surveying all is impractical.

practice1.q: Testing whether each parachute opens (the test destroys it) — census or sample?
practice1.hint: You can't destroy every one and still sell them.

practice1.q: The Australian national population count held every 5 years — census or sample?
A sample that reflects the whole population's mix is said to be ____.
True or false: a good sample must always be very large.
practice1.hint: A well-chosen representative sample can be small.

practice1.q: A chef tastes one spoonful to judge a whole pot of soup — census or sample?
practice1.hint: One well-mixed spoonful stands in for the whole pot.

practice2.q: A match is used up each time you test whether it lights, so the factory can't test them all. This kind of testing is called ____ testing.
practice2.hint: It destroys the item being tested — starts with 'd'.

practice2.q: A principal wants every student's favourite lunch in a school of 30. A census is practical here mainly because the population is ____.

Which is the BEST reason to sample rather than run a census when measuring all Australian teenagers' screen-time?
A. samples are always more accurate
B. the population is far too large to survey everyone
C. a census is illegal
D. samples don't need to be representative
Type the letter.
practice2.hint: Think about how many teenagers there are and what a census would cost.

practice2.q: A census includes everyone, so it is usually more ____ than a sample — but it costs far more.
practice2.hint: No estimation error when you measure everyone.

practice2.q: The Australian Census counts everyone because the government requires it. We say it is a census by ____.

A screen-time survey is given only to students in the school computer club. Why is this a poor sample?
A. it is too accurate
B. it is not representative of all teenagers
C. it is actually a census
D. it is destructive
Type the letter.
practice2.hint: Computer-club members probably use screens more than average — the sample is biased.

practice3.q:
A light-globe maker (2 million globes) wants average lifetime; testing burns out each globe tested. Best method and why?
A. census — it is the most accurate
B. sample — the test is destructive, so a census would leave nothing to sell
C. census — the population is too big for a sample to work
D. sample — any small group of globes will do
Type the letter.
practice3.hint: Destructive testing forces a sample; and a good sample needn't be huge, so C and D are wrong.

practice3.q: A manager says: 'Our sample of 500 mangoes stands in for the whole 50-tonne truckload, so we needn't check them all.' The property that makes this valid is that the sample is ____.
practice3.hint: It must fairly reflect the whole load.

practice3.q:
A student claims a sample must be at least half the population to be trusted. This claim is:
A. correct
B. incorrect — a well-chosen representative sample can be small
C. correct only for a census
D. correct only for destructive testing
Type the letter.
practice3.hint: This is today's central trap — size matters far less than being representative.

practice3.q:
Why does a national population count use a census rather than a sample?
A. counting everyone is cheap
B. the law requires an exact count of the whole population
C. the population is small
D. counting people is destructive
Type the letter.
practice3.hint: It's legally compulsory and needs an exact total.

exitProbs.q: A census collects data from ____ member of the population.
exitProbs.hint: Not just some — all of them.

exitProbs.q: Name one real situation where a census is impossible, and explain why sampling must be used instead.
exitProbs.hint: Think destructive testing (parachutes, matches, light globes) or a population that's far too large.

exitProbs.q: A classmate says: 'A sample is only trustworthy if it is very large.' Explain why this is wrong.
exitProbs.hint: Focus on being representative rather than being big.
